A new formulation of the Jacobian Conjecture in characteristic pp

Stefan Maubach Abdul Rauf Hogeschool Rotterdam Jacobs University Bremen Rotterdam, The Netherlands Bremen, Germany s.j.maubach@hr.nl a.rauf@jacobs-university.de Note: Supported by DAAD grant ( funding program ID 57076385).
Abstract

The Jacobian Conjecture uses the equation det(Jac⁡(F))∈k∗\det(\operatorname{Jac}(F))\in k^{*}, which is a very short way to write down many equations putting restrictions on the coefficients of a polynomial map FF. In characteristic pp these equations do not suffice to (conjecturally) force a polynomial map to be invertible. In this article, we describe how to construct the conjecturally sufficient equations in characteristic pp forcing a polynomial map to be invertible. This provides an (alternative to Adjamagbo’s formulation) definition of the Jacobian Conjecture in characteristic pp. We strengthen this formulation by investigating some special cases and by linking it to the regular Jacobian Conjecture in characteristic zero.

Keywords: the Jacobian Conjecture, positive characteristics, ideals.

1 Introduction

1.1 Notations and definitions

All rings are commutative with 1. We denote R[n]=R⁡[x1,…,xn]R^{[n]}=R[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}] the polynomial ring in nn variables over a ring RR. A polynomial map (or polynomial endomorphism) FF with coefficients in a ring RR is a list of polynomials (F1,…,Fn)(F_{1},\ldots,F_{n}) where Fi∈R[n]F_{i}\in R^{[n]}. Such a polynomial map provides an endomorphism of R[n]R^{[n]} as well as a map Rn⟶RnR^{n}\longrightarrow R^{n}. Since RR can be a finite field/ring, we cannot identify these viewpoints. (A polynomial map can induce the identity map Rn⟶RnR^{n}\longrightarrow R^{n} while not being the identity endomorphism.)

We define MEn⁡(R)\operatorname{ME}_{n}(R) as the set of polynomial endomorphisms on R[n]R^{[n]}. This forms a monoid w.r.t. composition, and the subset of invertible elements in this monoid is denoted by GAn⁡(R)\operatorname{GA}_{n}(R) and is the group of polynomial automorphisms. We define deg⁡(F)=max⁡(deg⁡(F1),…,deg⁡(Fn))\operatorname{deg}(F)=\max(\operatorname{deg}(F_{1}),\ldots,\operatorname{deg}(F_{n})) for F∈MEn⁡(R)F\in\operatorname{ME}_{n}(R). The set of affine automorphisms 𝐴𝑓𝑓n​(R)\mathit{Aff}_{n}(R) is {F∈GAn⁡(R)|deg⁡(F)=1}\{F\in\operatorname{GA}_{n}(R)~|~\operatorname{deg}(F)=1\}. A polynomial map F∈MEn⁡(R)F\in\operatorname{ME}_{n}(R) is triangular if Fi∈R⁡[xi,…,xn]F_{i}\in R[x_{i},\ldots,x_{n}]. If FF is a triangular automorphism and RR is a domain, it turns out to be of the form (r1​x1+f1,…,rn​xn+fn)(r_{1}x_{1}+f_{1},\ldots,r_{n}x_{n}+f_{n}) where ri∈R∗r_{i}\in R^{*} and fi∈k⁡[xi+1,…,xn]f_{i}\in k[x_{i+1},\ldots,x_{n}]. The set of triangular automorphisms is denoted by BAn⁡(R)\operatorname{BA}_{n}(R). Both BAn⁡(R)\operatorname{BA}_{n}(R) and 𝐴𝑓𝑓n​(R)\mathit{Aff}_{n}(R) turn out to be subgroups of GAn⁡(R)\operatorname{GA}_{n}(R). We define TAn⁡(R):=<BAn⁡(R),𝐴𝑓𝑓n​(R)>\operatorname{TA}_{n}(R):=<\operatorname{BA}_{n}(R),\mathit{Aff}_{n}(R)>, the tame automorphism group.

We define SAn⁡(R)={F∈GAn⁡(R)|det(Jac⁡(F))=1}\operatorname{SA}_{n}(R)=\{F\in\operatorname{GA}_{n}(R)~|~\det(\operatorname{Jac}(F))=1\}. Similarly, we define STAn⁡(R)=SAn⁡(R)∩TAn⁡(R)\operatorname{STA}_{n}(R)=\operatorname{SA}_{n}(R)\cap\operatorname{TA}_{n}(R) etc.

For each of these sets, we define MEnd⁡(R)={F∈MEn⁡(R)|deg⁡(F)≤d}\operatorname{ME}^{d}_{n}(R)=\{F\in\operatorname{ME}_{n}(R)~|~\operatorname{deg}(F)\leq d\}, GAd⁡(R)=GAn⁡(R)∩MEnd⁡(R)\operatorname{GA}^{d}(R)=\operatorname{GA}_{n}(R)\cap\operatorname{ME}_{n}^{d}(R) etc.

We use the notation xα=x1α1⋯xnαnx^{\alpha}=x_{1}^{\alpha_{1}}\cdots x_{n}^{\alpha_{n}} if α∈ℕn\alpha\in\mathbb{N}^{n}.

1.2 The Jacobian Conjecture

The Jacobian Conjecture is a quite notorious conjecture in the field of Affine Algebraic Geometry. One formulation is:

(JC(R,n)): If F∈MEn⁡(R)F\in\operatorname{ME}_{n}(R) where RR is a domain of characteristic zero, then det(Jac⁡(F))∈R∗\det(\operatorname{Jac}(F))\in R^{*} implies that F∈GAn⁡(R)F\in\operatorname{GA}_{n}(R).

For many details we can refer to the book [5]. The conjecture is widely open even in the case n=2n=2 (and trivial in dimension 1). Proving J​C​(R,n)JC(R,n) for any RR of characteristic zero yields J​C​(R,n)JC(R,n) true for all domains RR of characteristic zero.

Naievely translating the Jacobian Conjecture into characteristic pp yields counterexamples, already in dimension 1 even: the map x−xpx-x^{p} is not injective but has det(Jac⁡(x−xp))=1\det(\operatorname{Jac}(x-x^{p}))=1. Therefore, Adjamagbo defined in [4] a possible version of the Jacobian Conjecture for fields kk with characteristic char⁡(k)=p\operatorname{char}(k)=p:

(AJC(n,p)): Let F=(F1,…,Fn)F=(F_{1},\ldots,F_{n}) where Fi∈k⁡[x1,…,xn]F_{i}\in k[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}] and kk a field of characteristic pp. Assume that det(Jac⁡(F))∈k∗\det(\operatorname{Jac}(F))\in k^{*} and additionally assume that pp does not divide [k(x1,…,xn):k(F1,…,Fn)][k(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}):k(F_{1},\ldots,F_{n})]. Then FF has a polynomial inverse.

The “char⁡(k)\operatorname{char}(k) does not divide [k(x1,…,xn):k(F1,…,Fn)][k(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}):k(F_{1},\ldots,F_{n})]” requirement seems to exclude all pathological counterexamples to the Jacobian Conjecture, but adds another difficult requirement to the (deceptively simple looking but) difficult equation det(Jac⁡(F))∈k∗\det(\operatorname{Jac}(F))\in k^{*}. Adjamagbo showed that knowing A​J​C​(n,p)AJC(n,p) for all pp implies J​C​(n,k)JC(n,k) for all kk.

We approach the JC in characteristic pp from a different perspective: let us write down a generic polynomial automorphism of degree 2, having affine part identity:

F=(x+a1​x2+a2​x​y+a3​y2,y+b1​x2+b2​x​y+b3​y2)F=(x+a_{1}x^{2}+a_{2}xy+a_{3}y^{2},y+b_{1}x^{2}+b_{2}xy+b_{3}y^{2})

Then, in characteristic zero, the equation 1=det(Jac⁡(F))1=\det(\operatorname{Jac}(F)) yields several equations on the coefficients:

1=det(J​a​c​(F))=1+(2​a1+b2)​x+(a2+2​b3)​y+(2​a1​b2+2​a2​b1)​x2+(2​b2​a2+4​a1​b3+4​a3​b1)​x​y+(2​a2​b3+2​a3​b2)​y2\begin{array}[]{rl}1=&\det(Jac(F))\\ =&1+\\ &(2a_{1}+b_{2})x+\\ &(a_{2}+2b_{3})y+\\ &(2a_{1}b_{2}+2a_{2}b_{1})x^{2}+\\ &(2b_{2}a_{2}+4a_{1}b_{3}+4a_{3}b_{1})xy+\\ &(2a_{2}b_{3}+2a_{3}b_{2})y^{2}\\ \end{array}

Then apparently, the equations 2​a1+b2=0,2a_{1}+b_{2}=0, a2+2​b3=0a_{2}+2b_{3}=0, etc. are exactly the equations one needs to ensure that FF is invertible in characteristic zero. However, in characteristic 2 the above equations are not enough to conclude that FF is invertible (in fact, some equations completely vanish), as an example (x+x2,y)(x+x^{2},y) shows. Therefore, one needs extra equations in characteristic pp. In fact, thinking a little deeper, we know that such equations must exist. (Without going into detail, the equations must be the closure of the set of automorphisms having determinant Jacobian 1 inside MEnd⁡(k)\operatorname{ME}_{n}^{d}(k), where closure is in a natural topology [7, 8, 9]) We only have to find them. In this article we claim that we have found them (at least conjecturally). In fact, what we are doing is refining the regular Jacobian Conjecture so that it makes sense in characteristic pp also.

We make a remark on Adjamagbo’s formulation w.r.t. the above considerations: note that if there exists at least one counterexample FF to the Jacobian Conjecture in characteristic zero, then [k(x1,…,xn):k(F1,…,Fn)]=d>1[k(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}):k(F_{1},\ldots,F_{n})]=d>1. It might very well be that FmodpF\mod{p} is an interesting map for any prime pp. But, if p|dp|d, then Adjamagbo’s formulation excludes this example, while one could argue that a formulation of the JC in characteristic pp should not. One could say that in this case p∤[k(x1,…,xn):k(F1,…,Fn)]p\nmid[k(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}):k(F_{1},\ldots,F_{n})] adds too many equations, or perhaps the wrong equations.

2 Initial considerations

Let us consider the degree 2 example of the previous section. One of the equations is 2​a1​b2+2​a2​b22a_{1}b_{2}+2a_{2}b_{2}. In characteristic zero, this implies the equation a1​b2+a2​b1a_{1}b_{2}+a_{2}b_{1}. Looking at it like this, it seems strange to exclude this latter equation in characteristic 2. Also, if we define the ideal

I=(2​a1+b2,a2+2​b3,2​a1​b2+2​a2​b1,2​b2​a2+4​a1​b3+4​a3​b1,2​a2​b3+2​a3​b2)I=(2a_{1}+b_{2},a_{2}+2b_{3},2a_{1}b_{2}+2a_{2}b_{1},2b_{2}a_{2}+4a_{1}b_{3}+4a_{3}b_{1},2a_{2}b_{3}+2a_{3}b_{2})

in the ring ℚ⁡[a1​a2,a3,b1,b2,b3]\mathbb{Q}[a_{1}a_{2},a_{3},b_{1},b_{2},b_{3}], then any invertible polynomial map of degree 2 over ℚ\mathbb{Q} will have coefficients which satisfy any equation of II. Even more, they satisfy any equation appearing in rad⁡(I)\operatorname{rad}(I). Again, in the same vein as before, we can argue that any equation appearing in rad⁡(I)\operatorname{rad}(I), should appear as equation in characteristic pp, also. Hence, in this way we can give some universal equations which should be the equations which work in any characteristic.

This is essentially the formulation of the Jacobian Conjecture in characteristic pp we introduce in the next section, but we have to use more formal language.

3 A new formulation of the Jacobian Conjecture in characteristic pp

Given F=(F1,…,Fn)∈MEn⁡(R)F=(F_{1},\ldots,F_{n})\in\operatorname{ME}_{n}(R) where RR is some ring, we can write Fi=∑α∈ℕnci,α​xαF_{i}=\sum_{\alpha\in\mathbb{N}^{n}}c_{i,\alpha}x^{\alpha}. We can also make the infinitely generated ring CR:=R[ci,α|1≤i≤n,α∈ℕn]C_{R}:=R[c_{i,\alpha}~|~1\leq i\leq n,\alpha\in\mathbb{N}^{n}] where the ci,αc_{i,\alpha} are variables. One can now make the universal polynomial map of degree d∈ℕd\in\mathbb{N} by taking the polynomial map in MEn⁡(CR)\operatorname{ME}_{n}(C_{R}) which has coefficients the variables ci,αc_{i,\alpha}. Lets say that CR,dC_{R,d} is the finitely generated ring generated by the coefficients up to and including degree dd. (I.e. CRC_{R} is the union, or direct limit, of the rings …⊂CR,d⊂CR,d+1⊂…\ldots\subset C_{R,d}\subset C_{R,d+1}\subset\ldots. )

Definition 3.1.

Let F⁡[d]∈MEn⁡(Cℚ,d)F[d]\in\operatorname{ME}_{n}(C_{\mathbb{Q},d}) be the universal polynomial endomorphism of degree dd having affine part identity. Computing detJac⁡(F⁡[d])−1=∑α∈ℕnEα​xα\det\operatorname{Jac}(F[d])-1=\sum_{\alpha\in\mathbb{N}^{n}}E_{\alpha}x^{\alpha} yields a polynomial in x1,…,xnx_{1},\ldots,x_{n} having coefficients Eα∈Cℚ,dE_{\alpha}\in C_{\mathbb{Q},d}. Define the ideal Iℚd=(Eα|α∈ℕn)I_{\mathbb{Q}}^{d}=(E_{\alpha}~|~\alpha\in\mathbb{N}^{n}) in Cℚ,dC_{\mathbb{Q},d} generated by the equations found in the formula detJac⁡(F⁡[d])=1\det\operatorname{Jac}(F[d])=1. We define the ideal IℚI_{\mathbb{Q}} in CℚC_{\mathbb{Q}} as the inverse limit of the canonical chain …⟶Iℚd+1⟶Iℚd⟶…\ldots\longrightarrow I_{\mathbb{Q}}^{d+1}\longrightarrow I_{\mathbb{Q}}^{d}\longrightarrow\ldots. It coincides with the equations found in the coefficients of detJac⁡(F⁡[∞])=1\det\operatorname{Jac}(F[\infty])=1, where F⁡[∞]F[\infty] is the power series with universal coefficients.

Definition 3.2.

We define Jℤ:=rad⁡(Iℚ)∩CℤJ_{\mathbb{Z}}:=\operatorname{rad}(I_{\mathbb{Q}})\cap C_{\mathbb{Z}} as the “ideal of integer keller equations”. This ideal captures the universal equations described in the previous section. If RR is a ring, we define JR:=Jℤ⊗RJ_{R}:=J_{\mathbb{Z}}\otimes R as an ideal in the ring CRC_{R}. It is the ideal in CRC_{R} generated by those same equations (in characteristic zero) or by those equations modulo pp (in characteristic pp). In particular, we define Jp:=J𝔽p=JℤmodpJ_{p}:=J_{\mathbb{F}_{p}}=J_{\mathbb{Z}}\mod p as an ideal in C𝔽pC_{\mathbb{F}_{p}}. Similarly we define Jℤd:=rad⁡(Iℚd)∩Cℤ,d,J_{\mathbb{Z}}^{d}:=\operatorname{rad}(I_{\mathbb{Q}}^{d})\cap C_{\mathbb{Z},d}, JRd:=Jℤd⊗RJ_{R}^{d}:=J_{\mathbb{Z}}^{d}\otimes R and Jpd:=JℤdmodpJ_{p}^{d}:=J_{\mathbb{Z}}^{d}\mod p where d=d​e​g​(F).d=deg(F).

Let NdN_{d} be the number of variables in F⁡[d]F[d] (i.e. the dimension of the ring CR,dC_{R,d}). We say that v∈RNdv\in R^{N_{d}} satisfies JRdJ_{R}^{d} if f⁡(v)=0f(v)=0 for all f∈JRdf\in J_{R}^{d}. We say that “v∈RNdv\in R^{N_{d}} satisfies JRJ_{R}” if v∈RNdv\in R^{N_{d}} satisfies JRdJ_{R}^{d}.

We can identify F∈MEn⁡(R)F\in\operatorname{ME}_{n}(R) by the vector of coefficients v⁡(F)v(F) of FF; in particular, if F∈MEn⁡(R)F\in\operatorname{ME}_{n}(R) we say that “FF satisfies JRJ_{R} (JRdJ_{R}^{d})” if v⁡(F)v(F) satisfies JRJ_{R} (JRdJ_{R}^{d}).

Throughout, we will write the elements of JR=Jℤ⊗RJ_{R}=J_{\mathbb{Z}}\otimes R by ∑iei​hi\sum_{i}{e_{i}}h_{i} instead of ∑iei⊗hi\sum_{i}{e_{i}}\otimes h_{i}, where ei∈Jℤe_{i}\in J_{\mathbb{Z}} and hi∈Rh_{i}\in R for all ii (for simplicity, we will omit the tensor notation in this manuscript).

Definition 3.3.

We say that F∈MEn⁡(R)F\in\operatorname{ME}_{n}(R) is a strong Keller map if FF satisfies JRJ_{R} (or equivalently F∈MEn⁡(R)F\in\operatorname{ME}_{n}(R) is a strong Keller map if FF satisfies JRdJ_{R}^{d} where d​e​g​(F)=ddeg(F)=d). We denote the set of strong Keller maps by SKEn⁡(R)\operatorname{SKE}_{n}(R) and the set of Keller maps by KEn⁡(R).\operatorname{KE}_{n}(R).

Conjecture 3.4.

Jacobian conjecture over any field (in particular, in positive characteristics) (𝒥​𝒞​(𝐤,𝐧)\bf\mathcal{JC}(k,n))
Let kk be a field (of characteristic pp) and F∈MEn⁡(k)F\in\operatorname{ME}_{n}(k) be a strong Keller map. Then F∈GAn⁡(k)F\in\operatorname{GA}_{n}(k).

So, an alternative definition of 𝒥​𝒞​(k,n)\mathcal{JC}(k,n) is “SKEn⁡(k)=GAn⁡(k)\operatorname{SKE}_{n}(k)=\operatorname{GA}_{n}(k)”. We will use curly letter notation 𝒥​𝒞\mathcal{JC} to represent Jacobian conjecture in characteristic pp.

Of course, we still need to show that the above formulation coincides with the regular formulation in case the field is of characteristic zero. However, this will follow directly from lemma 4.3.

Note that we only defined the conjecture for fields of any characteristic, but with a slight modification one can define it for all domains (of any characteristic). However, we will stick with this formulation in this first encounter.

Before we will study the validity of this conjecture, we will introduce some facts and concepts we will use afterwards.

5 Two surjectivity conjectures

Given F∈GAn⁡(ℤ)F\in\operatorname{GA}_{n}(\mathbb{Z}) we can define FmodpF\mod p for any prime pp, yielding an element of GAn⁡(𝔽p)\operatorname{GA}_{n}(\mathbb{F}_{p}). If we additionally assume that p|det(Jac⁡(F))p\not|\det(\operatorname{Jac}(F)) then Fmodp∈GAn⁡(𝔽p)F\mod{p}\in\operatorname{GA}_{n}(\mathbb{F}_{p}), even. This yields the natural map π:SAn⁡(ℤ)⟶SAn⁡(𝔽p)\pi:\operatorname{SA}_{n}(\mathbb{Z})\longrightarrow\operatorname{SA}_{n}(\mathbb{F}_{p}). The following fact is not that difficult to prove:

Remark 5.1.

π⁡(STAn⁡(ℤ))=STAn⁡(𝔽p)\pi(\operatorname{STA}_{n}(\mathbb{Z}))=\operatorname{STA}_{n}(\mathbb{F}_{p}).

The reason for this is that (1) any affine or triangular map having determinant Jacobian 1 has a preimage under π\pi, (2) any tame automorphism of determinant Jacobian 1 can indeed be written as a composition of affine and triangular automorphisms of determinant Jacobian 1. (See [1] lemma 3.4.)

Now an obvious question is whether the map π:SAn⁡(ℤ)⟶SAn⁡(𝔽p)\pi:\operatorname{SA}_{n}(\mathbb{Z})\longrightarrow\operatorname{SA}_{n}(\mathbb{F}_{p}) is surjective or not; this question is interesting as nonsurjectivity would yield non-tame maps due to the above remark. This is part of the topic of the papers [1, 2, 3].

Definition 5.2.

Let RR be a ℤ\mathbb{Z} algebra and kk be a field such that we have a surjective ring homomorphism R⟶kR\longrightarrow k. We can extend it naturally from polynomial maps over RR to polynomial maps over k.k. We denote this extended map by π.\pi.

We notice that corresponding to each automorphism F∈SAn⁡(ℤ)F\in\operatorname{SA}_{n}(\mathbb{Z}) we have Fmodp∈SAn⁡(𝔽p),F\mod p\in\operatorname{SA}_{n}(\mathbb{F}_{p}), but there may exist some automorphisms f∈SAn⁡(𝔽p)f\in\operatorname{SA}_{n}(\mathbb{F}_{p}) such that π−1​(f)∉SAn⁡(ℤ).\pi^{-1}(f)\notin\operatorname{SA}_{n}(\mathbb{Z}). We conjecture the following for a ℤ\mathbb{Z} algebra RR and a field kk:

Conjecture 5.3.

Let RR be a ℤ\mathbb{Z} algebra and kk be any field. If we have a surjective ring homomorphism R⟶k,R\longrightarrow k, then we have

  1. 1.

    π⁡(SAn⁡(R))=SAn⁡(k)\pi(\operatorname{SA}_{n}(R))=\operatorname{SA}_{n}(k).

  2. 2.

    π−1​(SAn⁡(k))∩KEn⁡(R)=SAn⁡(R).\pi^{-1}(\operatorname{SA}_{n}(k))\cap\operatorname{KE}_{n}(R)=\operatorname{SA}_{n}(R).

A similar conjecture is the following (see also lemma 7.10 and corollary 7.11):

Conjecture 5.4.

Let RR be a ℤ\mathbb{Z} algebra and kk be any field of characteristic pp. If we have a surjective ring homomorphism R⟶k,R\longrightarrow k, then the map π:KEn⁡(R)⟶MEn⁡(k)\pi:\operatorname{KE}_{n}(R)\longrightarrow\operatorname{ME}_{n}(k) has SKEn⁡(k)\operatorname{SKE}_{n}(k) in its image.

If the above conjecture is not true, then it can mean various things: it could mean that 𝒥​𝒞​(k,n)\mathcal{JC}(k,n) is not true (or should be reformulated), or that there exist non-tame automorphisms over kk.

Assuming 𝒥​𝒞​(k,n)\mathcal{JC}(k,n) to be true, then conjecture 5.3 imples 5.4, but no other implications can be made, nor does 𝒥​𝒞​(k,n)\mathcal{JC}(k,n) imply any of the above conjectures.

Justification of the above conjectures: The above conjectures are not made to “match exactly what we need in our proofs”. They capture the essence of whether characteristic pp is truly different from characteristic zero. If one or more of these conjectures is wrong, then characteristic pp is in its core different from characteristic zero (for example, there might exist 𝔽p\mathbb{F}_{p}-automorphisms of 𝔽p[n]\mathbb{F}_{p}^{[n]} which are of a completely different nature than one can find in characteristic zero), while if both of them are correct, then characteristic pp is not too unsimilar from characteristic zero and both are intricately linked.

The tendency is to believe the conjectures (hence the name “conjecture” and not “problem” or “question”): it would be really surprising if any counterexamples would not be easily constructable in low degree and dimension (and known), whereas it can be easily imagined that the conjectures are true but hard to prove. For example, due to the the fact that we do not even have a (parametrized) list of generators for the automorphism group GAn⁡(k)\operatorname{GA}_{n}(k) (unlike for GLn⁡(k),TAn⁡(k)\operatorname{GL}_{n}(k),\operatorname{TA}_{n}(k)), we can understand that conjecture 5.4, if true, is very hard to prove. 11 1 Note, that with a little change, some people would agree on the same text for the Jacobian Conjecture.

Part 2: assuming invertibility satisfies the equations. Since we have a map in dimension 2, it is tame, and we can use the Jung-van der Kulk theorem. Since the degree is three or less, it is a map of the form α⁡(x,y+f⁡(x))​β\alpha(x,y+f(x))\beta where α,β\alpha,\beta are affine invertible maps, and deg⁡(f)≤3\operatorname{deg}(f)\leq 3. (There can only be one triangular map involved, as the degree is prime.) We can assume that β=(a​x+b​y+c,y)\beta=(ax+by+c,y) as we can put anything occuring in the second component in ff. Also, we can assume ff is of degree 2 or 3, and also we can assume that f⁡(0)=0f(0)=0 as we can put any constant added in α\alpha. Adding in the requirement that the affine part of α⁡(x,y+f⁡(x))​β\alpha(x,y+f(x))\beta must be the identity yields requirements on α\alpha given β\beta and f⁡(x)f(x). Working this out yields a generic map that is actually very similar to the formula of TT above; it can be easily checked that it satisfies the equations.

Remark: It is very hard to check this conjecture for specific degrees, even in n=2n=2, as there is no shortcut other than doing hard-core computations. In fact, en passant one is proving the conjecture, and the computations are very similar to proving the Jacobian Conjecture in characteristic zero - which is (we hope the reader agrees) a difficult task…

Of course, we also checked the conjecture for many specific examples (which we do not list here, though we specifically mention that we could rule out “obvious” examples like (x+xp,y)(x+x^{p},y)), though it feels a bit like touching a wall at random spots in the dark, not finding a light button and then shouting “this wall has no light button”.

7 Implications of the Jacobian Conjecture among various fields

In this section we will see if k,k´k,\acute{k} are two arbitrary fields of characteristics pp then what is the connection between 𝒥​𝒞​(k,n)\mathcal{JC}(k,n) and 𝒥​𝒞​(k´,n)\mathcal{JC}(\acute{k},n) for all n≥1.n\geq 1. We denote the Jacobian conjecture over all domains having characteristic zero by J​C​(n,0)JC(n,0) and the Jacobian conjecture over all fields with characteristic pp by 𝒥​𝒞​(n,p).\mathcal{JC}(n,p). In characteristics zero we have the following theorem (theorem 1.1.18 in [5]).

Theorem 7.1.

Let R,R´R,\acute{R} be commutative rings contained in a ℚ\mathbb{Q}-algebra. If J​C​(R,n)JC(R,n) is true for all n≥1,n\geq 1, then J​C​(R´,n)JC(\acute{R},n) is true for all n≥1n\geq 1.

For the characteristic pp equivalent we have to assume part of our conjectures:

Theorem 7.2.

Assume the conjectures 5.3(2), 5.4 are true. Let k,k´k,\acute{k} be two fields contained in an 𝔽p\mathbb{F}_{p}-algebra such that 𝒥​𝒞​(k,n)\mathcal{JC}(k,n) is true for all n≥1,n\geq 1, then 𝒥​𝒞​(k´,n)\mathcal{JC}(\acute{k},n) is true for all n≥1n\geq 1. In particular, it is enough to verify 𝒥​𝒞​(𝔽p,n)\mathcal{JC}(\mathbb{F}_{p},n).

It is very hard to prove the statement 7.2 without making any assumption. To mention the main hurdle: consider kk is infinite field and k1⊂kk_{1}\subset k a finite Galois extension, a1,a2,…,ana_{1},a_{2},\dots,a_{n} a k1k_{1} basis of kk and denote by α:k1m→k\alpha:k_{1}^{m}\rightarrow k the map defined by α⁡(y1,…,yn)=y1​a1+⋯+yn​an.\alpha(y_{1},\dots,y_{n})=y_{1}a_{1}+\dots+y_{n}a_{n}. The obvious extension (α,…,α):(k1m)n⟶kn(\alpha,\dots,\alpha):(k_{1}^{m})^{n}\longrightarrow k^{n} which we also denote by α,\alpha, is clearly bijective. Let F=(F1,…,Fn):kn⟶knF=(F_{1},\dots,F_{n}):k^{n}\longrightarrow k^{n} be a polynomial map. So conjugate FF with α\alpha we get the map Fα:=α−1​F​α:k1m​n⟶k1m​n.F^{\alpha}:=\alpha^{-1}F\alpha:k_{1}^{mn}\longrightarrow k_{1}^{mn}. Comparing to the characteristics zero proof of theorem 7.1 there we know that detJac⁡(F)∈k∗\det\operatorname{Jac}(F)\in k^{*} if and only if detJac⁡(Fα)∈k1∗\det\operatorname{Jac}(F^{\alpha})\in k_{1}^{*} (equation 1.1.26 in [5]). In characteristics pp we should have a similar statement that FF satisfies JkJ_{k} if and only if FαF^{\alpha} satisfies Jk1,J_{k_{1}}, but the proof of this is very difficult. This property that FF satisfies JkJ_{k} if and only if FαF^{\alpha} satisfies Jk1J_{k_{1}} is needed to prove the theorem 7.2 if we don’t assume that conjectures 5.3(2) and 5.4 are true. The remaining part of this section is devoted towards the proof of theorem 7.2. We begin with some definitions and lemmas.

Let Ω:=algebraic closure of ​𝔽p​({xi|i∈ℕ})\Omega:=\text{algebraic closure of }\mathbb{F}_{p}(\{x_{i}|i\in\mathbb{N}\}) then Ω\Omega is a field with infinite transcendence degree over 𝔽p.\mathbb{F}_{p}.

Definition 7.3.

Let R,SR,S be commutative rings. Let ϕ:R→S\phi:R\rightarrow S a ring homomorphism. If F∈R​[X]n,F\in R[X]^{n}, then FϕF^{\phi} denotes the element of S​[X]nS[X]^{n} obtained by applying ϕ\phi to the coefficients of the FiF_{i}.

We use the notation X=(x1,x2,…,xn).X=(x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{n}). The following proposition is taken from [5] (proposition 1.1.7 in [5]). η\eta is the nilradical of RR.

Proposition 7.4.

(Invertibility under base change) Let ϕ:R→S\phi:R\rightarrow S be a ring homomorphism with ker⁡ϕ⊂η.\operatorname{ker}\phi\subset\eta. Let F∈R​[X]nF\in R[X]^{n} with detJ​F​(0)∈R∗.\det JF(0)\in R^{*}. Then FF is invertible if and only if FϕF^{\phi} is invertible over S.S.

Lemma 7.5.

(Embedding lemma) Let 𝔽p⊂𝔽p​(a1,a2,…,an)\mathbb{F}_{p}\subset\mathbb{F}_{p}(a_{1},a_{2},\dots,a_{n}) be a finitely generated field extension. Then there exists an isomorphism ϕ:𝔽p​(a1,a2,…,an)≃k⊂Ω,\phi:\mathbb{F}_{p}(a_{1},a_{2},\dots,a_{n})\simeq k\subset\Omega, where kk is a subfield of Ω.\Omega.

To prove this lemma we will use the following lemma which can be seen in any standard textbook on algebra (theorem 2.8 on page 233 in [6]).

Lemma 7.6.

Let K/kK/k be an algebraic field extensions and let ϕ:k→C\phi:k\to C be a ring homomorphism where CC is an algebraically closed field. Then there exists a ring homomorphism σ:K→C\sigma:K\to C which extends ϕ.\phi.

Proof.

(of embedding lemma) As 𝔽p​(a1,a2,…,an)\mathbb{F}_{p}(a_{1},a_{2},\dots,a_{n}) is an algebraic extension of 𝔽p\mathbb{F}_{p} and we have an inclusion 𝔽p→Ω,\mathbb{F}_{p}\to\Omega, so it has an extension 𝔽p​(a1,a2,…,an)≃k⊂Ω\mathbb{F}_{p}(a_{1},a_{2},\dots,a_{n})\simeq k\subset\Omega by lemma 7.6. ∎

We can now use this to show that proving the 𝒥​𝒞\mathcal{JC} for Ω\Omega is universal, in the sense that it proves the Jacobian Conjecture for all fields of the same characteristic.

Proposition 7.7.

Let n≥1.n\geq 1. If 𝒥​𝒞​(Ω,n)\mathcal{JC}(\Omega,n) is true then 𝒥​𝒞​(k,n)\mathcal{JC}(k,n) is true for any field kk of characteristics p.p.

Proof.

Let F∈k​[X]nF\in k[X]^{n} satisfying Jℤ⊗k.J_{\mathbb{Z}}\otimes k. Let k0k_{0} be the subfield of kk generated over 𝔽p\mathbb{F}_{p} by the coefficients of F.F. Then FF satisfies Jℤ⊗k0.J_{\mathbb{Z}}\otimes k_{0}. By 7.5 we get an embedding ϕ:k0→Ω.\phi:k_{0}\to\Omega. Since FF satisfies Jℤ⊗k0J_{\mathbb{Z}}\otimes k_{0} we get that FϕF^{\phi} satisfies Jℤ⊗ϕ⁡(k0)J_{\mathbb{Z}}\otimes\phi(k_{0}) and hence by lemma 4.4 FϕF^{\phi} satisfies Jℤ⊗Ω.J_{\mathbb{Z}}\otimes\Omega. Hence FϕF^{\phi} is invertible over Ω\Omega since we assume that J​C​(Ω,n)JC(\Omega,n) is true. So by 7.4 FF is invertible over k0k_{0} and hence over k.k. ∎

Corollary 7.8.

of lemma 4.4
Let n≥1n\geq 1 and k0⊂kk_{0}\subset k be fields of characteristics p.p. If 𝒥​𝒞​(k,n)\mathcal{JC}(k,n) is true then 𝒥​𝒞​(k0,n)\mathcal{JC}(k_{0},n) is true for any subfield k0k_{0} of kk.

Proof.

Let F∈SKEn⁡(k0)F\in\operatorname{SKE}_{n}(k_{0}) then by lemma 4.4 we have F∈SKEn⁡(k).F\in\operatorname{SKE}_{n}(k). Since we assume that J​C​(k,n)JC(k,n) is true so FF is invertible over k.k. Hence FF is invertible over k0k_{0} by proposition 7.4. ∎

Let kk be any countable field of characteristics p. We can write k={a1,a2,…}k=\{a_{1},a_{2},\dots\} where each ai≠aja_{i}\neq a_{j} for all i≠j.i\neq j. We can also assume that kk is ordered set. Corresponding to each element aia_{i} in kk consider the indeterminate xi.x_{i}. Define a polynomial ring over ℤ\mathbb{Z} by Λk:=ℤ⁡[x1,x2,…].\Lambda_{k}:=\mathbb{Z}[x_{1},x_{2},...]. Define a map by τ:Λk→k\tau:\Lambda_{k}\rightarrow k by xi↦aix_{i}\mapsto a_{i} and m↦mmodpm\mapsto m\mod p for any m∈ℤ.m\in\mathbb{Z}. Then it is clearly well defined surjective ring homomorphism. Thus we have the following definition

Definition 7.9.

For each countable field kk of characteristics pp, define a polynomial ring Λk\Lambda_{k} over ℤ\mathbb{Z} such that τ:Λk⟶k\tau:\Lambda_{k}\longrightarrow k is surjective ring homomorphism.

Notice that we can naturally extend τ\tau to a map from polynomial maps over Λk\Lambda_{k} to polynomial maps over kk. We denote this extended map by π\pi as in definition 5.2.

Thus we have the following lemma.

Lemma 7.10.

Let kk be a countable field of characteristics p.p. We have π⁡(KEn⁡(Λk))⊆SKEn⁡(k)\pi(\operatorname{KE}_{n}(\Lambda_{k}))\subseteq\operatorname{SKE}_{n}(k) for every n≥1.n\geq 1.

Proof.

Let F∈KEn⁡(Λk),F\in\operatorname{KE}_{n}(\Lambda_{k}), then detJac⁡(F)=1\det\operatorname{Jac}(F)=1 and so FF satisfies IℚI_{\mathbb{Q}}. Let q∈Jk:=J¯ℤ⊗kq\in J_{k}:=\bar{J}_{\mathbb{Z}}\otimes k then q=∑iei~​hiq=\sum_{i}\tilde{e_{i}}h_{i} for ei~∈J¯ℤ\tilde{e_{i}}\in\bar{J}_{\mathbb{Z}} and hi∈kh_{i}\in k for all ii (here e~i​hi=e~i⊗hi,\tilde{e}_{i}h_{i}=\tilde{e}_{i}\otimes h_{i}, but we omit the tensor notation). Since hi∈kh_{i}\in k there exist Hi∈ΛkH_{i}\in\Lambda_{k} such that τ⁡(Hi)=hi.\tau(H_{i})=h_{i}. Thus there exist Q∈JΛkQ\in J_{\Lambda_{k}} defined by Q=∑iei​HiQ=\sum_{i}{e_{i}}H_{i} such that q=∑iτ⁡(ei)​τ​(Hi)=∑iei~​hiq=\sum_{i}\tau(e_{i})\tau(H_{i})=\sum_{i}\tilde{e_{i}}h_{i} where ei∈Jℤe_{i}\in J_{\mathbb{Z}} such that τ⁡(ei)=ei~\tau(e_{i})=\tilde{e_{i}} for all ii. By lemma 4.2 we have ei​(ν​(F))=0e_{i}(\nu(F))=0 for all ii (since FF satisfies IℚI_{\mathbb{Q}}). If we identify xix_{i} with aia_{i} as in definition of τ,\tau, ei~​(ν⁡(π⁡(F)))=ei​(ν⁡(F))modp=0modp\tilde{e_{i}}(\nu(\pi(F)))=e_{i}(\nu(F))\mod p=0\mod p for all i.i. Thus q⁡(ν⁡(π⁡(F)))=∑iei~​(ν⁡(π⁡(F)))​hi​(ν⁡(π⁡(F)))=0modp.q(\nu(\pi(F)))=\sum_{i}\tilde{e_{i}}(\nu(\pi(F)))h_{i}(\nu(\pi(F)))=0\mod p. This shows that π⁡(F)\pi(F) satisfies Jk.J_{k}. Hence π⁡(F)∈SKEn⁡(k)\pi(F)\in\operatorname{SKE}_{n}(k) which proves the lemma.

∎

Of course, the above lemma slightly reformulates conjecture 5.4:

Corollary 7.11.

Assume conjecture 5.4 is true and kk be a countable field of characteristics p.p. Then π⁡(KEn⁡(Λk))=SKEn⁡(k).\pi(\operatorname{KE}_{n}(\Lambda_{k}))=\operatorname{SKE}_{n}(k).

We are now ready to link J​C​(n,0)JC(n,0) to 𝒥​𝒞​(n,p)\mathcal{JC}(n,p).

Proposition 7.12.

(1) Assume conjecture 5.4 is true. Then

J​C​(n,0)​∀n∈ℕ∗⟹𝒥​𝒞​(n,p)​∀n∈ℕ∗.JC(n,0)\forall n\in\mathbb{N}^{*}\Longrightarrow\mathcal{JC}(n,p)\forall n\in\mathbb{N}^{*}.

(2) Assume the conjectures 5.3(2), 5.4 are true. Then

J​C​(n,0)​∀n∈ℕ∗⟺𝒥​𝒞​(n,p)​∀n∈ℕ∗.JC(n,0)\forall n\in\mathbb{N}^{*}\Longleftrightarrow\mathcal{JC}(n,p)\forall n\in\mathbb{N}^{*}.

In fact, it is enough to prove or disprove J​C​(n,ℤ)JC(n,\mathbb{Z}) for all nn to prove or disprove 𝒥​𝒞​(k,n)\mathcal{JC}(k,n) for all nn and for any field kk.

Proof.

(1) Consider KK be an arbitrary field of characteristics pp and f∈S​Kn​(K).f\in SK_{n}(K). Let kk be a subfield of KK generated over 𝔽p\mathbb{F}_{p} by the coefficients of f.f. Since kk is at most countable, we have a surjective ring homomorphism τ:Λk→k\tau:{\Lambda_{k}}\rightarrow k (definition 7.9). By corollary 7.11 there exists F∈KEn⁡(Λk)F\in\operatorname{KE}_{n}({\Lambda_{k}}) such that π⁡(F)=f\pi(F)=f. Thus FF is invertible since we assume that J​C​(n,0)JC(n,0) is true, so there exist G∈MEn⁡(Λk)G\in\operatorname{ME}_{n}(\Lambda_{k}) such that F∘G=I.F\circ G=I. Applying π\pi we have π⁡(F)∘π⁡(G)=π⁡(I)=Imodp.\pi(F)\circ\pi(G)=\pi(I)=I\mod p. Thus π⁡(G)\pi(G) is an inverse of f=π⁡(F).f=\pi(F). This shows that ff is invertible over kk and hence over K.K.
(2) Let KK be an arbitrary field of characteristics pp and consider k⊆Kk\subseteq K be a countable field (if K is itself countable then take k=Kk=K). By corollary 7.11 we have π⁡(KEn⁡(Λk))=SKEn⁡(k)\pi(\operatorname{KE}_{n}({\Lambda_{k}}))=\operatorname{SKE}_{n}(k) (where Λk\Lambda_{k} is defined in 7.9). Let F∈KEn⁡(Λk)F\in\operatorname{KE}_{n}({\Lambda_{k}}) then π⁡(F)\pi(F) satisfies Jk.J_{k}. Suppose 𝒥​𝒞​(K,n)\mathcal{JC}(K,n) is true then 𝒥​𝒞​(k,n)\mathcal{JC}(k,n) is true by corollary 7.8. Thus π⁡(F)∈SAn⁡(k)\pi(F)\in\operatorname{SA}_{n}(k) and so F∈π−1​(SAn⁡(k)).F\in\pi^{-1}(\operatorname{SA}_{n}(k)). By conjecture 5.3(2) we have F∈SAn⁡(Λk).F\in\operatorname{SA}_{n}({\Lambda_{k}}). By theorem 7.1 we have that J​C​(n,0)JC(n,0) is true. ∎

Proof.

(of theorem 7.2)
This is direct consequence of proposition 7.12 ∎

8 Some results related to 𝒥​𝒞​(k,n)\mathcal{JC}(k,n)

In this section we present some basic results related to our formulation of the Jacobian conjecture in characteristic pp.

8.1 Invertible polynomial maps and 𝒥​𝒞​(k,n)\mathcal{JC}(k,n)

In this subsection we will discuss a natural question which can come to mind when studying the previous. If characteristic of kk is zero then we know that if F∈SAn⁡(k)F\in\operatorname{SA}_{n}(k) then FF satisfies the keller condition detJac⁡(F)=1\det\operatorname{Jac}(F)=1 (the only condition for Jacobian conjecture J​C​(k,n)JC(k,n)). This is due to the fact that the determinant of the Jacobian has the property detJac⁡(G∘F)=detJac⁡(F)⋅(detJac⁡(G)∘F)\det\operatorname{Jac}(G\circ F)=\det\operatorname{Jac}(F)\cdot(\det\operatorname{Jac}(G)\circ F). If characteristic of kk is pp it is not easy to prove that if F∈SKEn⁡(k)F\in\operatorname{SKE}_{n}(k) then FF satisfies JkJ_{k} (the universal equations).

Nevertheless, assuming conjectures 5.3(1) and 5.4 we can prove that if F∈SAn⁡(k)F\in\operatorname{SA}_{n}(k) then it implies that F∈SKEn⁡(k).F\in\operatorname{SKE}_{n}(k).

Proposition 8.1.

Assume conjectures 5.3(1) and 5.4 are true and kk be a field of characteristics p.p. If f∈SAn⁡(k)f\in\operatorname{SA}_{n}(k) then f∈SKEn⁡(k).f\in\operatorname{SKE}_{n}(k).

Proof.

Let f∈SAn⁡(k).f\in\operatorname{SA}_{n}(k). Consider k0⊂kk_{0}\subset k generated over 𝔽p\mathbb{F}_{p} by the coefficients of f.f. By conjecture 5.3(1) there exist some F∈SAn⁡(Λk0)F\in\operatorname{SA}_{n}(\Lambda_{k_{0}}) such that π⁡(F)=f\pi(F)=f and thus FF satisfies KEn⁡(Λk0).\operatorname{KE}_{n}(\Lambda_{k_{0}}). Assuming conjecture 5.4 we have π⁡(KEn⁡(Λk0))=SKEn⁡(k0)\pi(\operatorname{KE}_{n}(\Lambda_{k_{0}}))=\operatorname{SKE}_{n}(k_{0}) by corollary 7.11. Thus f∈SKEn⁡(k0)f\in\operatorname{SKE}_{n}(k_{0}) and hence f∈SKEn⁡(k)f\in\operatorname{SKE}_{n}(k) by lemma 4.4. ∎

8.2 Closure property of SKEn⁡(k)\operatorname{SKE}_{n}(k)

The set KEn⁡(R)\operatorname{KE}_{n}(R) is closed under composition for any ring RR, and also for R=kR=k a field of characteristic pp, even though it does not only consist of automorphisms. One would expect that SKEn⁡(𝔽p)\operatorname{SKE}_{n}(\mathbb{F}_{p}) is also closed under composition. However, trying to prove this turns out to be an incredibly difficult task: if F∈SKEn⁡(𝔽p)F\in\operatorname{SKE}_{n}(\mathbb{F}_{p}) then the coefficients of FF satisfy certain equations that can be found in JpJ_{p}. If we compose two such maps F,G∈SKEn⁡(𝔽p)F,G\in\operatorname{SKE}_{n}(\mathbb{F}_{p}), then the coefficients of the resulting map F∘GF\circ G (denoted v⁡(F∘G)v(F\circ G)) are polynomials in the coefficients of FF and GG, i.e. v⁡(F∘G)=P⁡(v⁡(F),v⁡(G))v(F\circ G)=P(v(F),v(G)) for some polynomial map PP. To check if F∘GF\circ G is in SKEn⁡(𝔽p)\operatorname{SKE}_{n}(\mathbb{F}_{p}) we need to see if v⁡(F∘G)v(F\circ G) satisfy (the equations in) JpJ_{p}; however, this turned out to be extremely difficult.

Comparing to characteristic zero, there we know a priori due to the “magical” equation detJac⁡(F∘G)=detJac⁡(G)⋅(detJac⁡(F)∘G)\det\operatorname{Jac}(F\circ G)=\det\operatorname{Jac}(G)\cdot(\det\operatorname{Jac}(F)\circ G) that KEn⁡(ℤ)\operatorname{KE}_{n}(\mathbb{Z}) is closed under composition. As a corollary, it gives that “v⁡(F)v(F) satisfies JℤJ_{\mathbb{Z}} and v⁡(G)v(G) satisfies JℤJ_{\mathbb{Z}}” implies “v⁡(F∘G)v(F\circ G) satisfies JℤJ_{\mathbb{Z}}”, but exactly how is very complicated.

Nevertheless, making an assumption we can prove that SKEn⁡(𝔽p)\operatorname{SKE}_{n}(\mathbb{F}_{p}) is closed under composition.

Proposition 8.2.

Assume conjecture 5.4 is true. Then SKEn⁡(k)\operatorname{SKE}_{n}(k) is closed under composition, where kk be any field of characteristics pp.

Proof.

Let f,g∈SKEn⁡(k).f,g\in\operatorname{SKE}_{n}(k). Let k1k_{1} be the subfield of kk generated over 𝔽p\mathbb{F}_{p} by the coefficients of ff and gg. Field k1k_{1} is countable, thus by corollary 7.11 there exist F,G∈KEn⁡(Λk1)F,G\in\operatorname{KE}_{n}(\Lambda_{k_{1}}) such that π⁡(F)=f\pi(F)=f and π⁡(G)=g\pi(G)=g. Now F∘G∈KEn⁡(Λk1)F\circ G\in\operatorname{KE}_{n}(\Lambda_{k_{1}}) as KEn⁡(Λk1)\operatorname{KE}_{n}(\Lambda_{k_{1}}) is closed under composition. Thus by corollary 7.11 f∘g=π⁡(F)∘π⁡(G)=π⁡(F∘G)∈SKEn⁡(k1).f\circ g=\pi(F)\circ\pi(G)=\pi(F\circ G)\in\operatorname{SKE}_{n}(k_{1}). Hence f∘g∈SKEn⁡(k)f\circ g\in\operatorname{SKE}_{n}(k) (lemma 4.4). ∎

8.3 Connections between 𝒥​𝒞​(𝔽p,n)\mathcal{JC}(\mathbb{F}_{p},n) and J​C​(ℤ,n)JC(\mathbb{Z},n).

In this subsection we will see how we can move back and forth between 𝒥​𝒞​(𝔽p,n)\mathcal{JC}(\mathbb{F}_{p},n) and J​C​(ℤ,n).JC(\mathbb{Z},n). We quote theorem 10.3.13 from [5]. We will need this theorem to build the connection between 𝒥​𝒞​(𝔽p,n)\mathcal{JC}(\mathbb{F}_{p},n) and J​C​(ℤ,n)JC(\mathbb{Z},n).

Theorem 8.3.

Let F∈ℤ​[x1,x2,…,xn]n.F\in\mathbb{Z}[x_{1},x_{2},\dots,x_{n}]^{n}. If Fmodp:𝔽pn→𝔽pnF\mod p:{\mathbb{F}_{p}}^{n}\rightarrow{\mathbb{F}_{p}}^{n} is injective for all but finitely many primes pp and detJac⁡(F)∈ℤ∖{0},\det\operatorname{Jac}(F)\in\mathbb{Z}\setminus\{0\}, then FF is invetible over ℤ.\mathbb{Z}.

Lemma 8.4.

If 𝒥​𝒞​(𝔽p,n)\mathcal{JC}(\mathbb{F}_{p},n) is true for all but finitely many primes pp, then J​C​(ℤ,n)JC(\mathbb{Z},n) is true.

This is a slight variation on proposition 7.12 but without any requirements.

Proof.

Let F∈MEn⁡(ℤ),F\in\operatorname{ME}_{n}(\mathbb{Z}), such that det(Jac⁡(F))=1.\det(\operatorname{Jac}(F))=1. Then by lemma 7.10 FmodpF\mod p satisfies Jp.J_{p}. Thus FmodpF\mod p is invertible for almost all pp by given assumptions. By theorem 8.3 we conclude that FF is invertible. ∎

For the converse of this lemma we need to assume conjecture 5.4 to be true. This in turn resembles proposition 7.12.

Lemma 8.5.

Suppose conjecture 5.4 and J​C​(ℤ,n)JC(\mathbb{Z},n) are true, then 𝒥​𝒞​(𝔽p,n)\mathcal{JC}(\mathbb{F}_{p},n) is true.

Proof.

Let f∈MEn⁡(𝔽p)f\in\operatorname{ME}_{n}(\mathbb{F}_{p}) such that ff satisfies Jp.J_{p}. By corollary 7.11 there exists F∈KEn⁡(ℤ)F\in\operatorname{KE}_{n}(\mathbb{Z}) such that Fmodp=fF\mod p=f. By assumption, FF is invertible, so there exist G∈MEn⁡(ℤ)G\in\operatorname{ME}_{n}(\mathbb{Z}) such that F∘G=I.F\circ G=I. Thus (Fmodp)∘(Gmodp)=Imodp(F\mod p)\circ(G\mod p)=I\mod p and hence Gmodp:=gG\mod p:=g is the inverse of ff. ∎

8.4 Boundedness

In this subsection we explore what happens if we assume that if the degree, or the degree and the coefficents, of a polynomial map is small with respect to pp. In some sense, the results say that if pp is “small” with respect to some formula depending on pp and nn, then the situation is exactly the same as in characteristic zero. We fix nn in this section, but note that the constant NdN_{d} below depends also on nn.

Let MEn⁡(𝔽p)d\operatorname{ME}_{n}{({\mathbb{F}}_{p})}^{d} be the set of polynomial endomorphisms of degree at most d.d. Similarly we can define KEn⁡(𝔽p)d,\operatorname{KE}_{n}(\mathbb{F}_{p})^{d}, SKEn⁡(𝔽p)d\operatorname{SKE}_{n}(\mathbb{F}_{p})^{d} etc.

Lemma 8.6.

Let F∈M​En​(𝔽p)dF\in ME_{n}{({\mathbb{F}}_{p})}^{d} and IQd=(E1,…,Em)I_{Q}^{d}=(E_{1},\dots,E_{m}) then there exist a positive integer NdN_{d} such that for p>Ndp>N_{d} we have Jℤ(p)d=rad⁡(E1,…,Em).J_{\mathbb{Z}_{(p)}}^{d}=\operatorname{rad}(E_{1},\dots,E_{m}).

Proof.

Consider the ideals Iℚd=(E1,…,Em)I_{\mathbb{Q}}^{d}=(E_{1},\dots,E_{m}) and Iℚd∩Cℤ(p)=(E1,…,Em,Q1,…,Qr),I_{\mathbb{Q}}^{d}\cap C_{\mathbb{Z}_{(p)}}=(E_{1},\dots,E_{m},Q_{1},\dots,Q_{r}), where Qi=Pi​(E1,…,Em)ni,Q_{i}=\frac{P_{i}(E_{1},\dots,E_{m})}{n_{i}}, and Pi​(X)P_{i}(X) are polynomials with integer coefficients. Let Nd=l​c​m​(n1,n2,…,nr).N_{d}=lcm(n_{1},n_{2},\dots,n_{r}). Then for p>Ndp>N_{d} we have Iℚd∩CR=(E1,…,Em)I_{\mathbb{Q}}^{d}\cap C_{R}=(E_{1},\dots,E_{m}) where R:=ℤ⁡[1Nd].R:=\mathbb{Z}[\frac{1}{N_{d}}]. Hence Jℤ(p)d:=rad⁡(Iℚd∩CR)=rad⁡(E1,…,Em).J_{\mathbb{Z}_{(p)}}^{d}:=\operatorname{rad}(I_{\mathbb{Q}}^{d}\cap C_{R})=\operatorname{rad}(E_{1},\dots,E_{m}). ∎

Corollary 8.7.

Let F∈M​En​(𝔽p)dF\in ME_{n}{({\mathbb{F}}_{p})}^{d} and Iℚd=(E1,…,Em)I_{\mathbb{Q}}^{d}=(E_{1},\dots,E_{m}) then there exist a positive integer NdN_{d} such that for p>Ndp>N_{d} we have Jpd=rad⁡(E1modp,…,Emmodp).J_{p}^{d}=\operatorname{rad}(E_{1}\mod p,\dots,E_{m}\mod p).

Proof.

Since by definition

Jpd=Jℤdmodp=Jℤd⊗ℤ𝔽pJ_{p}^{d}=J_{\mathbb{Z}}^{d}\mod p=J_{\mathbb{Z}}^{d}\otimes_{\mathbb{Z}}\mathbb{F}_{p}
=Jℤd⊗ℤ(ℤ(p)⊗ℤ(p)𝔽p)=J_{\mathbb{Z}}^{d}\otimes_{\mathbb{Z}}(\mathbb{Z}_{(p)}\otimes_{\mathbb{Z}_{(p)}}\mathbb{F}_{p})
=(Jℤd⊗ℤℤ(p))⊗ℤ(p)𝔽p=(J_{\mathbb{Z}}^{d}\otimes_{\mathbb{Z}}\mathbb{Z}_{(p)})\otimes_{\mathbb{Z}_{(p)}}\mathbb{F}_{p}
=Jℤ(p)d⊗ℤ(p)𝔽p=J_{\mathbb{Z}_{(p)}}^{d}\otimes_{\mathbb{Z}_{(p)}}\mathbb{F}_{p}
=Jℤ(p)dmodp.=J_{\mathbb{Z}_{(p)}}^{d}\mod p.

By lemma 8.6 we get Jpd=Jℤ(p)dmodp=rad⁡(E1modp,…,Emmodp).J_{p}^{d}=J_{\mathbb{Z}_{(p)}}^{d}\mod p=\operatorname{rad}(E_{1}\mod p,\dots,E_{m}\mod p). ∎

Corollary 8.8.

There exist a positive integer NdN_{d} such that KEn⁡(ℤ)dmodp⊂SKEn⁡(𝔽p)d\operatorname{KE}_{n}(\mathbb{Z})^{d}\mod p\subset\operatorname{SKE}_{n}(\mathbb{F}_{p})^{d} for p>Nd.p>N_{d}.

Proof.

Direct consequence of corollary 8.7. ∎

The following lemma is intuitively clear: if you have a polynomial map having coefficients which are (in ℤ\mathbb{Z}) small, then knowing that the map modulo pp is a (special) Keller map yields that it was a Keller map to start with.

Lemma 8.9.

Let f∈SKEn⁡(𝔽p)df\in\operatorname{SKE}_{n}(\mathbb{F}_{p})^{d} having coefficients bounded by some constant C,C, (meaning here that for the coefficients a representative in ℤ\mathbb{Z} can be picked in the interval [−C,C][-C,C]). If pp is large enough with respect to dd and C,C, then picking F∈M​En​(ℤ)dF\in ME_{n}(\mathbb{Z})^{d} such that f=Fmodpf=F\mod p and the coefficients of FF are in the interval [−C,C][-C,C], then F∈KEn⁡(ℤ)d.F\in\operatorname{KE}_{n}(\mathbb{Z})^{d}.

Proof.

Consider ideals Iℚd=(E1,…,Em)I_{\mathbb{Q}}^{d}=(E_{1},\dots,E_{m}) and Iℚd∩Cℤ,d=(Q1,…,Qr)I_{\mathbb{Q}}^{d}\cap C_{\mathbb{Z},d}=(Q_{1},\dots,Q_{r}) such that Qi=Pi​(E1,…,Em)ni,Q_{i}=\frac{P_{i}(E_{1},\dots,E_{m})}{n_{i}}, where Pi​(X)P_{i}(X) are polynomials with integer coefficients for all ii. Let Nd=l​c​m​(n1,n2,…,nr)N_{d}=lcm(n_{1},n_{2},\dots,n_{r}) then for p>Ndp>N_{d} we have Iℚd∩CR,d=(E1,…,Em)I_{\mathbb{Q}}^{d}\cap C_{R,d}=(E_{1},\dots,E_{m}) where R=ℤ⁡[1Nd].R=\mathbb{Z}[\frac{1}{N_{d}}]. Let f∈SKEn⁡(𝔽p)df\in\operatorname{SKE}_{n}(\mathbb{F}_{p})^{d} then s⁡(ν⁡(f))=0modps(\nu(f))=0\mod p for all s∈Jpd.s\in J_{p}^{d}. Consider S∈JRdS\in J_{R}^{d} such that Smodp=sS\mod p=s and F∈MEn⁡(ℤ)F\in\operatorname{ME}_{n}(\mathbb{Z}) such that Fmodp=fF\mod p=f then S⁡(ν⁡(F))modp=0modpS(\nu(F))\mod p=0\mod p for all S∈JRd.S\in J_{R}^{d}. Since Iℚd∩CR,d⊂JRdI_{\mathbb{Q}}^{d}\cap C_{R,d}\subset J_{R}^{d} thus for p>Ndp>N_{d} we have Ei​(ν⁡(F))modp=0modpE_{i}(\nu(F))\mod p=0\mod p for all i.i. Define Ni:=max{|Ei(η)|:η∈[C,C]l,l=the number of coefficients of the generic polynomial F}N_{i}:=\max\{|E_{i}(\eta)|:\eta\in[C,C]^{l},l=\text{the number of coefficients of the generic polynomial F}\} and Nd​(C):=max⁡{Nd,N1,N2,…,Nm},N_{d}(C):=\max\{N_{d},N_{1},N_{2},\dots,N_{m}\}, then for p>Nd​(C)p>N_{d}(C) we have |Ei​(ν⁡(F))|<p|E_{i}(\nu(F))|<p for all 1≤i≤m.1\leq i\leq m. Thus Ei​(ν​(F))=0E_{i}(\nu(F))=0 for all 1≤i≤m1\leq i\leq m for p>Nd​(C).p>N_{d}(C). Hence F∈KEn⁡(ℤ)dF\in\operatorname{KE}_{n}(\mathbb{Z})^{d} for p>Nd​(C).p>N_{d}(C). ∎

Under some very stringent conditions we can now show closedness under composition of some elements in SKEn⁡(𝔽p)\operatorname{SKE}_{n}(\mathbb{F}_{p}). Let MEn⁡(𝔽p)d,C\operatorname{ME}_{n}{({\mathbb{F}}_{p})}^{d,C} be the set of polynomial endomorphisms of degree at most dd with bounded coefficients (indeed we can choose CC large enough and for bound coefficients are considered as representative in ℤ\mathbb{Z}). Similarly we can define KEn⁡(𝔽p)d,C\operatorname{KE}_{n}(\mathbb{F}_{p})^{d,C} SKEn⁡(𝔽p)d,C\operatorname{SKE}_{n}(\mathbb{F}_{p})^{d,C} etc.

Corollary 8.10.

There exist a positive integer Nd2​(C)N_{d^{2}}(C) such that if f,g∈SKEn⁡(𝔽p)d,Cf,g\in\operatorname{SKE}_{n}(\mathbb{F}_{p})^{d,C} with p>Nd2​(C)p>N_{d^{2}}(C) then f∘g∈SKEn⁡(𝔽p)d2,C.f\circ g\in\operatorname{SKE}_{n}(\mathbb{F}_{p})^{d^{2},C}.

Proof.

Let f,g∈SKEn⁡(𝔽p)d,Cf,g\in\operatorname{SKE}_{n}(\mathbb{F}_{p})^{d,C} such that for F,G∈MEn⁡(ℤ),F,G\in\operatorname{ME}_{n}(\mathbb{Z}), Fmodp=fF\mod p=f and Gmodp=g.G\mod p=g. By lemma 8.9 for p>Nd2​(C)p>N_{d^{2}}(C) we have F,G∈KEn⁡(ℤ)d,C.F,G\in\operatorname{KE}_{n}(\mathbb{Z})^{d,C}. Since KEn⁡(ℤ)d,C\operatorname{KE}_{n}(\mathbb{Z})^{d,C} is closed under composition. Thus F∘G∈KEn⁡(ℤ)d2,C.F\circ G\in\operatorname{KE}_{n}(\mathbb{Z})^{d^{2},C}. Hence by corollary 8.7 for p>Nd2​(C)p>N_{d^{2}}(C) we have f∘g∈SKEn⁡(𝔽p)d2,C.f\circ g\in\operatorname{SKE}_{n}(\mathbb{F}_{p})^{d^{2},C}. ∎

The generic case eludes us:

Conjecture 8.11.

Let kk be a field of characteristic pp. Then SKEn⁡(k)\operatorname{SKE}_{n}(k) is closed under composition.
